By
Cornelius Timmermann, senior consultant, Lignum Consulting Inc.

How frameless construction and connected production opens the next growth chapter for US cabinetry

By
Cornelius Timmermann, senior consultant, Lignum Consulting Inc.

Walk through a well-run face-frame cabinet plant in the U.S. today, and you will increasingly find both ends of the production spectrum under one roof. At one end, a disciplined kanban system keeps racks full of components, face frames, and doors, built in advance for orders that have not yet arrived. At the other end, a frameless line builds only what has been ordered, cabinet by cabinet.

The kanban side works, and it took years to get right. It also ties up capital in parts that sit idle and limits the product range to what the plant can afford to stock. As customers ask for more variety and shorter lead times, inventory that waits for demand becomes cash that isn't working.

That contrast sums up where U.S. cabinetry stands. The industry built its efficiency on stock production and the face frame. Its customers now want custom cabinets delivered fast and at a fair price. At Lignum Consulting, we see frameless construction produced to order as the most direct way for U.S. manufacturers to meet that demand on an industrial scale.
Three vantage points shape how we read the U.S. market: the technology on offer, the way plants are organized today, and what homeowners buy. All three now point the same way.
On the technology side, batch-size-one panel processing, automated part sorting and connected shop-floor software are proven technology, sold and serviced in the U.S.
In manufacturing organization, the industry is in transition. Stock systems built over decades now face pressure from custom demand, and frameless lines increasingly run to order right beside them.

In the showroom, demand tells the same story. In its February trend report, Woodworking Network noted that figures are hard to come by, but frameless construction appears to be growing and is roughly “neck-and-neck” with face-frame construction among U.S. manufacturers. It already dominates in Canada. The same report observed that many U.S. face-frame cabinets now carry full-overlay doors that make them “outwardly indistinguishable from their Euro competitors.”
Three vantage points, one direction. Technology, organization and demand all point toward frameless cabinets built to order.
That last point matters. When the frame no longer shows, the choice between the two constructions becomes less about appearance and more about how each one fits the plant's production system.
The market has already voted for custom

IBISWorld puts U.S. cabinet and vanity manufacturing at $22.1 billion in 2025. Custom cabinets are the largest segment at $9.3 billion, or 42% of revenue, ahead of stock and pre-made kitchen cabinets at $8.2 billion. Domestic stock sales have lost ground to imports from Canada, Mexico, Vietnam and Malaysia. Custom work has gained, because overseas plants struggle to match exact dimensions, finishes and delivery windows.
Custom cabinets are already the largest product segment. Source: IBISWorld (January 2026); shares of $22.1 billion total.

For most countries of origin, imported kitchen cabinets and vanities carry a 25% Section 232 tariff, and the increase to 50% has been postponed to January 1, 2027. The tariff helps domestic producers today, but policy can change.
IBISWorld also expects industry revenue to stay essentially flat through 2030. In a flat market, growth means taking share, and the share on offer is in custom work delivered fast. U.S. plants can compete on cost, too. Labor is the cost the market sees as high, but in a well-automated frameless plant it makes up only about 10% of total production cost. Imports, meanwhile, carry freight, duty and weeks of goods in transit that a domestic plant avoids.
Face frame and frameless: what each asks of the plant

The face frame is a hardwood frame, typically 1.5 inches wide, glued and nailed to the front of the cabinet box. It gives American cabinets their character and makes installation forgiving. It also adds a second, solid-wood production chain alongside the panel line.

A frameless cabinet is built entirely from flat panels, drilled to a standard hole pattern known as the 32mm system. A face-frame cabinet needs the same panels, in the same material and finish, plus a solid-wood frame with its own material, machines and labor. On a typical base cabinet with one door and one drawer, the frame adds five solid-wood parts (two stiles and three rails) and six joints.
With full-overlay doors, a face-frame cabinet looks like a frameless one. The difference stays on the plant floor. Schematic of an 18-inch base cabinet.

Those five parts go through nine extra operations before the cabinet ships. Figure 4 compares the two constructions step by step, like for like: same box material, same end panels, same doors. The only variable is the frame.

On the panel side, the two constructions are close. Both start from the same box panels, whether prefinished melamine or veneer, and both cut, bore, and assemble a box. The frameless line edgebands the front edges, bores the 32mm hole pattern on the CNC, and inserts dowels before the case clamp. The face-frame line grooves and bores, leaving the front edges for the frame. If the box is veneer, it is sanded and finished the same way in both. The finished end panels and doors are identical, too.

The difference is the frame. Its five parts start as rough lumber and go through rough milling, molding, cutting to length, joinery, and frame assembly. The frame is then machine-sanded and hand-sanded, puttied and touched up, glued and nailed to the box, and flush-sanded at the joints. Finally, it is finished and color-matched to the doors and end panels. That is the only extra finishing step face-frame construction adds.

The frame also shapes hardware and installation. Face-frame hinges are specific to the frame, and drawer slides need spacers or rear brackets to clear it. In a frameless box, cup hinges and slides mount directly on the 32mm line. At installation, the frame is forgiving because it hides small deviations, while frameless cabinets rely on accurate boxes and leveling legs. For automation, the box runs in batch size one in either construction, but the frame is harder to automate and still involves more manual handling. In a frameless plant, nearly every step can run at batch size one.

Simplified operations sequence for a base cabinet box. The face frame adds nine operations, most of them in solid wood; the only extra finishing step is the frame itself. The chart counts operations, not labor hours or lead time.

In a face-frame plant, most labor sits in solid wood and finishing, the two areas hardest to automate and staff. That weighs heavily in an industry where, according to IBISWorld, wages already take 23% of revenue, against 12% across all manufacturing. Sanding and finishing are typically among the most labor-intensive departments, and face frames tend to sit near the bottom of the automation roadmap because solid-wood parts resist the data-driven flow that panels handle easily. Frameless construction doesn't change how the box, end panels or doors are finished, but it takes the frame out of that chain.

The face frame remains the right choice for many products. Inset doors and traditional designs depend on it, and installers nationwide know it well. The Kitchen Cabinet Manufacturers Association notes that frameless cabinets require more precise installation because no frame can hide small box deviations. The question is not which construction is better, but which one fits the product. Where the design calls for a frame, it adds real value. In full-overlay kitchens, frameless delivers the same look with fewer operations and more room for automation.

Frameless construction also changes the economics of variety. When every part is a data-defined panel, a 27-inch cabinet takes the machine no more effort than a 24-inch one. The width that fits the customer's wall becomes the standard product.
Customization stops driving cost and becomes a data problem, and data problems scale.

Kanban-driven make-to-stock production works well when demand is predictable, and variety is low. Forecasts and replenishment signals trigger production, and efficiency comes from run length and volume. Components run in batches, finished cabinets wait in a warehouse, and orders pull from stock. The costs show up as capital tied up in components and finished goods, warehouse space, obsolete styles and colors, and a product range limited to what the business can afford to stock.
Make-to-order production reverses the trigger: customer orders start production. Parts are cut in batch size one, sorted and sequenced by order, assembled and shipped just in time. Any size within the product rules can be built, inventory shrinks to raw material and purchased parts, and efficiency depends on data quality and flow rather than run length. Kanban doesn't disappear. It moves upstream. Hardware, edgebanding, and raw panels still flow best through supermarkets and pull signals, while the product itself follows the customer order.

Not every plant needs to jump straight to full batch-size-one production. The key design decision is the customer order decoupling point, the step where production switches from forecast to order. Figure 5 shows three typical positions. In pure make-to-stock, the decoupling point sits just before shipping, and finished cabinets wait in a warehouse. In a parts-to-stock, assemble-to-order plant, panels are cut, edgebanded and drilled to forecast, then held in a sorting buffer until an order pulls them into assembly. In full make-to-order, the decoupling point moves ahead of panel cutting, and every step runs to the customer order. The right point depends on product mix, order profile and available capital, and it shapes most of the investment case.
Where the decoupling point sits decides how much of the plant runs to order. Adapted from Lignum Consulting plant concepts.
The supply base is already here
Little of this has to be built from scratch. The networks behind frameless production have been growing in the US for decades.

Hardware. European hinge and drawer-system makers run US headquarters, distribution and, in some cases, local production. One founded its US subsidiary in 1973. For another, the US is now its largest single market worldwide.
Machinery. The major panel-processing machinery groups sell, install and service batch-size-one lines in North America, with local technicians and spare parts.
Panels. US plants produce particleboard, MDF and thermally fused laminate at scale.
Software. Design, CAD/CAM, configurator and MES platforms built around the 32mm system are available and supported here.
Every component of a frameless kitchen is already on US shelves. Most plants lack a production system that turns those components into custom cabinets at industrial speed.
What it takes: the Connected Factory
The Connected Factory: seven building blocks for a make-to-order plant.
Buying a nesting router or a batch-size-one edgebander doesn't create a make-to-order plant. Lignum Consulting approaches the transition through the Connected Factory and its seven building blocks.
Strategy. Define markets, channels, lead times and the decoupling point.
Product. Build rule-based construction principles and a clean product data model, so custom sizes flow through without engineering on every order.
Technology. Match machinery and automation to the product rules and volumes. Lignum Consulting has no financial ties to machine or software vendors.
Logistics. Plan material flow, part sorting and sequencing so every order reaches assembly complete and ships in route sequence.
Digitalization. Connect sales, design, ERP, CAM and MES into one data thread, with no re-keying.
Organization. Realign planning, scheduling and quality around order-driven flow.
People. Train operators, planners and installers, especially crews moving from face-frame to frameless installation.
Buying machines before defining the product. Automation multiplies whatever it receives. Without rule-based product data, a batch-size-one line produces batch-size-one errors.
Building the business case on tariffs. A plant designed to win on lead time, fit and cost keeps winning when trade policy changes.
Treating frameless as a catalog addition. A frameless line added to a face-frame plant, without new planning, scheduling and installer support, creates two half-systems.

Start with an honest look at the current plant: where orders come from, where the decoupling point sits today, which data exists, and how far the current layout and equipment can go. Lignum Consulting's Connected Factory Assessment delivers that picture and a phased roadmap.
Homeowners have already told the market what they want. The plants that can build those kitchens to order, at industrial cost and with short lead times, will be the ones taking share.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Cornelius Timmermann is a Senior Consultant at Lignum Consulting Inc. A trained cabinetmaker with a B.Eng. from TH Rosenheim, he came up through the shop floor and remains closely connected to the industry. He has been with Lignum Consulting for four years and works on its US team.
